design_detail: Within-person laboratory study on a residential research unit in 9 men who used both injected and smoked cocaine. Phase I: eight sessions at least 48 hours apart (intravenous cocaine hydrochloride 0, 8, 16 and 32 mg; smoked cocaine base sham, 12.5, 25 and 50 mg), doses in ascending order within each route, route order counterbalanced across participants, with cuff blood pressure, heart rate and spoken visual-analogue ratings and no blood sampling. Phase II: two test days at least a week apart, one per route, each with that route's four doses in ascending order about 90 minutes apart; for the two highest doses, radial-artery and venous blood were drawn at the same moments at 23 times from 5 minutes before to 90 minutes after dosing, with continuous invasive arterial blood pressure. Both routes were given over 15 seconds. Order: nothing was randomized; the order of the two phase II test days is not reported. Blinding: participants were blindfolded while smoking so as not to see the amount in the pipe; no other blinding is described, and the route was evident. Participants: men currently using both routes, not described as seeking treatment. Analyses use only the two highest doses of each route in phase II (n = 7 to 9).
can_establish: In 8–9 men who used both injected and smoked cocaine, how radial-artery and venous plasma cocaine concentrations differ over 90 minutes after 16 and 32 mg injected and 25 and 50 mg smoked over 15 seconds, sampled at the same moments, and how blood pressure, heart rate and three rated effects changed over the first 10 minutes.
cannot_establish: Whether smoked cocaine reaches the brain sooner or at higher concentration than injected cocaine (brain levels were not measured and arterial samples were 15 seconds apart); whether either route is more addictive or more toxic; or whether smoked cocaine has a greater effect per unit of blood concentration (doses rose in a fixed order, the smoked dose actually delivered is unknown, and sham and placebo responses were not taken into account).

sample.recruitment: Not described. Adult male volunteers with current use of both intravenous and smoked cocaine, paid for participation, who lived on the Clinical Research Unit of the Addiction Research Center (National Institute on Drug Abuse), Baltimore, for about 5 weeks; treatment seeking is not mentioned (pp. 1345–1346).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Current histories of both intravenous and smoked cocaine use; no other significant medical or psychiatric disorder on physical examination, electrocardiogram, clinical blood chemistry, urinalysis and psychological interview; informed consent; consent form and procedures approved by the Institutional Review Board under Department of Health and Human Services guidelines. An Allen test confirmed adequate collateral circulation to the hand before arterial catheterization (pp. 1346–1347).
sample.demographics: Of the 9 completers, 7 African-American and 2 Caucasian men; mean age 34 years (range 24–45); mean weight 73 kg (61–92). They had used both routes for an average of 7.5 years and reported using each at least two or three times a week in the previous month, spending about $200 and using about 2.5 g of cocaine a week on average; all used other drugs, with cocaine their main drug (p. 1346).
sample.attrition: 13 started; 4 were medically discharged in phase I: 3 for transient premature ventricular contractions (two of whom had received only intravenous placebo) and 1 for chest pain after a single 25 mg smoked dose (p. 1346). Of the 9 completers, one was removed from all analyses because his plasma concentrations after smoking were minimal, which the authors take to mean he did not inhale the drug, and another repeated the smoked test day and had blood drawn only for the first 10 minutes after the two highest doses (p. 1348).
sample.selection_effects: Men only, mostly African-American, experienced with both injecting and smoking cocaine, which limits how far the route comparison applies to people who use one route only or less often. The completers are those who tolerated every dose in phase I without arrhythmia or chest pain, and the participant who apparently did not inhale was removed, so the analysed group is selected for tolerance and for effective smoking under the study's procedure.

exposure.measurement: Drug given in the laboratory; cocaine measured in arterial and venous plasma (about 2.5 ml per sample, in tubes with sodium fluoride and acetic acid preservative, plasma frozen at −30 °C) by solid-phase extraction and gas chromatography–mass spectrometry; sensitivity about 1 ng/ml, between-assay coefficient of variation 5.4% (n = 15) (p. 1347). Participants' own use by self-report only (p. 1346).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: intravenous cocaine hydrochloride (USP) 0, 8, 16 or 32 mg in 1.0 ml, injected over 10 seconds and followed by a 5-second saline flush; smoked cocaine base (described as crack or free-base cocaine, prepared under the direction of the centre's chief pharmacist and chief chemist and analysed by gas chromatography–mass spectrometry for purity before use) sham, 12.5, 25 or 50 mg from a modified pipe, in one staff-timed administration of 15 seconds (pp. 1346–1347). The amount of smoked cocaine actually inhaled was not measured. In phase II each route's four doses were given on one day in ascending order about 90 minutes apart (pp. 1346–1347). At the mean weight of 73 kg the 16 and 32 mg injected and 25 and 50 mg smoked doses are about 0.22, 0.44, 0.34 and 0.68 mg/kg (editors' calculation). Participants reported using about 2.5 g a week (p. 1346).
exposure.polysubstance: All participants used other drugs, which are neither named nor quantified; residence on the unit for the study's 5 weeks is the only control described, and no drug testing during the study is reported (p. 1346).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Residential throughout. Phase I sessions were at least 48 hours apart and the phase II test days at least 1 week apart. Within a test day, residual cocaine from the preceding dose was present before the analysed doses: mean 9.1 and 21.2 ng/ml before 16 and 32 mg injected, and 0.0 and 24.4 ng/ml before 25 and 50 mg smoked (p. 1348).

comparison.controls: Within-person comparisons: arterial against venous samples drawn at the same moments; injected against smoked cocaine on separate days; medium against high dose within a day. Intravenous placebo and sham smoking were given as the first session of each sequence but are not included in any analysis.
comparison.matching: Within-person design; the routes were matched on administration time (15 seconds) and on doses chosen from earlier studies to give similar venous concentrations (p. 1346), but the venous concentrations reached after smoking were lower than expected (p. 1353).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to the concentration questions. For effects, the pre-dose value in each session is the only baseline; tolerance from heavy use, and acute tolerance within the ascending-dose day, were not measured.

outcomes.instruments: Plasma cocaine (arterial and venous). Phase I: cuff blood pressure, heart rate and continuous electrocardiogram. Phase II: continuous invasive radial-artery systolic and diastolic pressure, heart rate, electrocardiogram and pulse oximetry. Six visual-analogue questions (stimulated, high, anxious, sedated, down, drug liking) answered aloud with a number from 0 to 100, because both arms were in use (p. 1347).
outcomes.validity_norms: The assay's sensitivity and between-assay precision are reported; spoken 0–100 ratings depart from standard written scales and have no norms. Invasive pressures run higher than cuff pressures, as the authors note, so phase II values are not comparable with cuff values from other studies (p. 1347).
outcomes.operationalization: Peak value and time to peak per person; time course of arterial against venous concentrations; variance in each effect explained by arterial or venous concentration at 0.25 and 4 minutes; hysteresis plotted from group means. Nothing is operationalized as harm or toxicity.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None: about 15 outcome measures (peak and time to peak of concentration, the concentration time course, and peak and time to peak of three cardiovascular measures and three ratings) were analysed by repeated-measures ANOVAs with several factors each, plus 48 regression tests in Table 1, all at P ≤ .05 with the Huynh-Feldt correction for sphericity only (p. 1348). Three of the six ratings (anxious, sedated, down) are reported only as essentially unchanged, without data (p. 1350).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: None: a physician gave the injections, doses rose in a fixed order, and participants knew the route and spoke their ratings aloud to staff. The assay and the monitored values are objective.

analysis.effect_sizes: F statistics and P values for the ANOVAs and r² with P for the regressions; no confidence intervals or standardized effect sizes. Peak concentrations: high dose above medium, F(1,7) = 22.058, P < .0022; injected above smoked, F(1,7) = 7.613, P < .0281; arterial above venous, F(1,7) = 91.353, P < .0001; arterial peaks earlier than venous, F(1,7) = 52.158, P < .0002, with no difference in time to peak by route or dose (p. 1348). Mean arterial concentration 15 seconds after 32 mg injected 2347 ng/ml against venous 27 ng/ml (p. 1352); venous peaks 108 and 252 ng/ml after 16 and 32 mg injected and 67 and 143 ng/ml after 25 and 50 mg smoked (pp. 1353–1354). At 0.25 minutes arterial concentration explained 63% (injected) and 69% (smoked) of the variance in systolic pressure, venous concentration 12% and 9% (not significant) (Table 1, p. 1353).
analysis.covariates: None; within-person ANOVAs. The regressions combine the two highest doses of each route, two observations per person, as if they were independent (p. 1348; Table 1, footnote b, p. 1353).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol registration or pre-specified primary outcome is mentioned; portions of the results were presented at the College on Problems of Drug Dependence in June 1994 (p. 1345).
analysis.selective_reporting: Only the two highest doses of each route are analysed; placebo, sham and the lowest doses, given in the same sequences, appear in figures but are never analysed, so no effect is tested against placebo or sham. The regression time points (0.25 and 4 minutes) were chosen as the observed concentration peaks (p. 1348). Three of the six ratings are not shown.
analysis.power: Not reported; 7 to 9 men. Non-significant route differences in peak effects therefore cannot be read as equivalence.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 8–9 men who used both routes, radial-artery cocaine concentrations rose during the 15-second administration and peaked at the 15-second sample after both routes, at about ten times the venous peak, which came at about 4 minutes; the two converged within about 20 minutes. Smoked doses of 25 and 50 mg gave lower arterial and venous concentrations than injected doses of 16 and 32 mg, while peak blood pressure, heart rate and ratings did not differ significantly between routes. Arterial concentration at 15 seconds explained more of the variance in effects than venous concentration, which had barely begun to rise at that time.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract infers from similar effects at lower concentrations that smoked cocaine may produce a greater effect at similar concentrations (p. 1345), but the routes were compared on raw peaks without reference to the sham and placebo sessions, although sham smoking itself raised systolic pressure and ratings of high (Figs 3 and 5, pp. 1350, 1352), and the similar means are non-significant differences in 8 people. The abstract's conclusion that faster arrival at the brain does not explain greater effects after smoking (p. 1345) becomes in the Discussion summary the statement that "this study determined that smoked cocaine does not reach the brain faster than i.v. cocaine" (p. 1356); brain arrival was not measured, the arterial samples were 15 seconds apart, and the authors themselves allow that a larger bolus may reach the brain in the first circuit after smoking (p. 1353). The Discussion says the results confirm a physiological kinetic model (p. 1355) on the strength of untested differences in r² from regressions that pool two doses per person, and suggests that people may experience greater and potentially more toxic effects than venous sampling and traditional monitoring estimate (p. 1356), which no measure in the study addresses. The authors state the main design limits openly: ascending dose order, active participation in smoking against passive injection, and invasive monitoring (p. 1355).

timeline.event: Barnett et al.: intravenous 100 and 200 mg in four men, with blood drawn from the other arm from 5 minutes, when the first sample held the highest measured concentration; no arterial sampling.

Foltin and Fischman (as described here, pp. 1346, 1354–1355): with the same doses and pipe, 25 and 50 mg smoked gave venous concentrations and cardiovascular effects similar to 16 and 32 mg injected, and greater rated effects after smoking at similar venous concentrations; venous concentrations 4 minutes after a first dose of 25 or 50 mg smoked were about 150 and 200 ng/ml.
Foltin and Fischman (as described here, p. 1355): in a choice study, 50 mg smoked was chosen more often than either injected dose.
Henningfield et al. (as described here, p. 1346): arterial nicotine concentrations during and after smoking a cigarette substantially exceeded venous concentrations, in some people tenfold.
Cone (as described here, p. 1355): ratings of high and liking were greater after smoked than injected cocaine at doses giving nearly identical peak venous concentrations.
Booze et al. (in press at the time; as described here, p. 1353): in rats, arterial cocaine concentrations peaked 30 seconds after intravenous injection.

replication.where_it_stands: By the authors' account the first measurement of arterial cocaine concentrations in humans; no repeat of the arterial-venous comparison was read for this card. Its finding of similar effects after the two routes despite lower concentrations after smoking runs against earlier studies with the same doses, which found greater effects after smoking at similar venous concentrations (Foltin and Fischman, 1991, 1992; Cone, 1995, as described here); the authors attribute the difference partly to their restricted smoking procedure and to invasive monitoring (pp. 1354–1355).

funding.funder: Supported by the National Institute on Drug Abuse/National Institute of Mental Health; carried out in the Intramural Research Program of the National Institute on Drug Abuse; portions presented at the College on Problems of Drug Dependence, West Palm Beach, FL, in June 1994 (p. 1345, footnote 1).
funding.affiliations_note: All authors at the Addiction Research Center, National Institute on Drug Abuse, National Institutes of Health, Baltimore; the first author's later address is the New York State Psychiatric Institute and Columbia University (p. 1345). The acknowledgements thank Dr. Richard W. Foltin for data analyses (p. 1356); Foltin is an author of the earlier studies whose doses and pipe this study adopted and with which its results are compared. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A crossover with randomized order of routes and doses, the delivered smoked dose measured, injected and smoked doses matched on arterial exposure, sham and placebo sessions used as comparators, and either brain uptake measured directly or arterial sampling resolved at intervals of a few seconds, in a sample that includes women and people who use only one route.

domains.domain: Randomization process (order of routes and doses)
domains.note: Nothing was randomized. Within each route the doses rose in a fixed order on one day, so dose is confounded with time of day, residual cocaine (up to 24.4 ng/ml before the high doses) and acute tolerance; the order of the two phase II test days is not reported (only the phase I route order was counterbalanced). The arterial-venous comparison, made on samples drawn at the same moments, is not affected.

Participants and staff knew the route; the blindfold hid only the amount in the pipe. The smoked dose actually delivered is unknown, and the concentrations it produced were lower than expected; one participant who apparently did not inhale was removed from all analyses and another repeated the smoked day. The authors note that active participation in smoking, against passive injection, may itself have raised effects (p. 1355).

4 of 13 men left in phase I, before any blood was drawn; the analyses use 7 to 9 of the 9 completers, and the numbers differ between figures and tests (for example, drug liking: N = 7 in Fig. 5 but F(1,7), implying 8, in the text, pp. 1350, 1352).

The assay and monitored values are objective (low on their own), but phase II pressures were measured invasively and run higher than cuff values, the termination limit for systolic pressure was relaxed by 30–40 mm Hg in phase II (p. 1347), and ratings were spoken aloud to staff by participants who knew the route.

No protocol. Only the two highest doses are analysed, placebo and sham never; the regression time points were chosen at the observed concentration peaks; three ratings are not reported; the regression P values fit a degrees-of-freedom figure that does not match 16 observations, and one F statistic above the 5% critical value is reported as non-significant (see reporting issues).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The arterial-venous comparison, made on samples drawn at the same moments in the same people, is the study's strongest and least biased result. The comparisons between routes and between doses are at high risk: doses rose in a fixed order, the order of the route days is unreported, the delivered smoked dose is unknown, participants knew the route, and no effect is compared with placebo or sham. The source can be cited for the time course of radial-artery against venous cocaine concentrations after 16–32 mg injected and 25–50 mg smoked over 15 seconds in 8–9 men who used both routes, for arterial peaks at the 15-second sample after both routes, and for the point that venous samples taken minutes later miss the early arterial peak. It cannot be cited for statements that smoked cocaine does or does not reach the brain faster, for the relative potency of the routes per unit concentration, or for toxicity or addictiveness.

key_findings.finding: Of 13 men who started, 4 were medically discharged during phase I: 3 for transient premature ventricular contractions, two of whom had received only intravenous placebo, and 1 for chest pain after a single 25 mg smoked dose.
key_findings.note: Phase I had cuff blood pressure and a continuous electrocardiogram but no arterial line; the events are reported without further detail.

key_findings.finding: The 9 completers (7 African-American and 2 Caucasian men; mean age 34 years, range 24–45; mean weight 73 kg) had used both intravenous and smoked cocaine for an average of 7.5 years, each route at least two or three times a week in the previous month, and reported using about 2.5 g of cocaine a week.

Study conditions: both routes were given over 15 seconds, intravenous cocaine hydrochloride 0, 8, 16 or 32 mg (10-second injection plus 5-second flush) and smoked cocaine base sham, 12.5, 25 or 50 mg in one staff-timed administration; in phase II each route's doses were given in ascending order about 90 minutes apart, and arterial and venous samples were drawn together from 5 minutes before to 90 minutes after the two highest doses, including samples 5 seconds into administration, at its end and 0.25, 0.5 and 1 minute after.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Design and General Procedures, 2nd to 4th paragraphs (pp. 1346–1347); Drug Administration (p. 1347)

key_findings.finding: Peak arterial concentrations were higher than peak venous concentrations (F(1,7) = 91.353, P < .0001) and came sooner (F(1,7) = 52.158, P < .0002): mean arterial concentrations peaked about 15 seconds after the end of administration and venous concentrations about 4 minutes after, with no significant difference in time to peak by route or dose.
key_findings.locator: Results › Cocaine plasma concentrations, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Fifteen seconds after 32 mg intravenous cocaine, mean arterial concentration was 2347 ng/ml and mean venous concentration 27 ng/ml; at the sample taken 5 seconds into the 15-second administration, arterial and venous concentrations were similar.
key_findings.note: Arterial peaks for the other doses are shown only in Fig. 1 (p. 1349). Read from the figure (editors, approximate): about 1350 ng/ml after 16 mg injected, 1100 after 25 mg smoked and 1650 after 50 mg smoked, all at the 15-second sample.

key_findings.finding: Peak venous concentrations were 108 and 252 ng/ml after 16 and 32 mg injected and 67 and 143 ng/ml after 25 and 50 mg smoked, at about 4 minutes; injected doses gave higher peak concentrations than smoked doses (F(1,7) = 7.613, P < .0281), and high doses higher than medium doses (F(1,7) = 22.058, P < .0022).
key_findings.locator: Results › Cocaine plasma concentrations, 1st paragraph (p. 1348); Discussion, 4th paragraph (p. 1353) and 5th paragraph (begins p. 1353; these values on p. 1354)
key_findings.note: In Fig. 1 (p. 1349) the mean venous curve after 25 mg smoked is nearly flat at about 60–66 ng/ml from 4 to 10 minutes (editors' reading), so the 4-minute peak time is nominal for that dose.

key_findings.finding: Arterial and venous concentrations then converged and declined at similar rates; they no longer differed significantly within 20 minutes after injected (F(1,7) = 5.755, reported as P > .05) or smoked doses (F(1,7) = 3.538, P > .05), and at 90 minutes concentrations after the highest doses were still above those after the medium doses.
key_findings.locator: Results › Cocaine plasma concentrations, 2nd paragraph; Fig. 2 (p. 1349)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: F(1,7) = 5.755 corresponds to P = .048, below the paper's threshold of P ≤ .05 (see reporting issues). The smoked time course uses 7 participants.

key_findings.finding: Residual cocaine from the dose given 90 minutes earlier was present before the analysed doses: mean 9.1 and 21.2 ng/ml before 16 and 32 mg injected, and 0.0 and 24.4 ng/ml before 25 and 50 mg smoked.

In phase I (cuff), mean peak systolic pressure after the highest doses was 158 mm Hg (32 mg injected) and 154 mm Hg (50 mg smoked), at the first reading about 1 minute after dosing. In phase II (arterial line), peak systolic pressure did not differ significantly between the two highest doses of either route or between routes, was 20 to 40 mm Hg above the cuff values, and peaked at 0.84 minutes on average.
key_findings.locator: Results › Cardiovascular effects of cocaine, 1st paragraph (p. 1348) and 2nd paragraph (pp. 1348–1349)
key_findings.note: The same paragraph also gives 10–15 mm Hg for the phase I–phase II difference. Read from Fig. 3 (editors, approximate; no error bars shown for phase II): phase II mean peaks of about 175 mm Hg after 32 mg injected and about 181–183 after 50 and 25 mg smoked; in phase II, sham smoking also raised mean systolic pressure from about 137 to about 165 mm Hg at the end of administration, against about 143 to 155 after intravenous placebo.

key_findings.finding: Peak diastolic pressure was higher after 32 than 16 mg injected (F(1,7) = 20.525, P < .0027) but not significantly higher after 50 than 25 mg smoked, and peaked at about 1 minute with no significant difference in timing by dose or route; heart rate peaked at around 107 beats per minute after the highest dose of either route, was higher after 32 than 16 mg injected (F(1,7) = 8.198, P < .0242), rose as much after 25 as after 50 mg smoked, and peaked at 1.45 minutes on average.
key_findings.locator: Results › Cardiovascular effects of cocaine, 3rd paragraph (p. 1349, continuing on p. 1350)

key_findings.finding: Ratings of stimulated, high and drug liking peaked at about 1.0 to 1.5 minutes and did not differ significantly in peak or timing between routes. The high dose raised peak liking after both routes (injected F(1,7) = 14.704, P < .0064; smoked F(1,7) = 10.468, P < .0143) and peak stimulated only after injection (F(1,7) = 7.006, P < .0331); high did not differ between doses. Ratings stayed raised for about 10 minutes, were low by 15 to 30 minutes and absent by 90 minutes; anxious, sedated and down were essentially unchanged.
key_findings.locator: Results › Subjective effects of cocaine, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The drug-liking panels of Fig. 5 (p. 1352) show N = 7 for each route. Read from Fig. 5 (editors, approximate): sham smoking produced mean high ratings of about 16 of 100, against about 5 after intravenous placebo.

key_findings.finding: At 0.25 minutes, arterial concentration explained 63% (injected) and 69% (smoked) of the variance in systolic pressure and venous concentration 12% and 9% (not significant); at 4 minutes, arterial and venous concentrations explained 76% and 62% after injection but 24% (P = 0.046) and 4% (not significant) after smoking. For ratings of stimulated, high and liking, arterial concentration at 0.25 minutes explained 45% to 63% of the variance after either route, whereas venous concentration at 0.25 minutes after smoking explained 1% (not significant).
key_findings.locator: Results › Relationship of cocaine plasma concentrations and cardiovascular effects, 1st paragraph (p. 1350, continuing on p. 1351); Table 1 (p. 1353)
key_findings.note: Each regression pools the two highest doses of a route, two observations per person, and the footnote gives df = 15 for what should be 16 observations from 8 people (see reporting issues). At 0.25 minutes venous concentration had barely begun to rise, so a low venous r² at that time is expected by construction.

key_findings.finding: Plotted against arterial concentration, cardiovascular effects and ratings showed counterclockwise hysteresis, and against venous concentration clockwise hysteresis; after smoking, heart rate rose at once, dipped transiently at 0.25 minutes (which the authors suggest may be a Valsalva response to the inhalation) and rose again.
key_findings.locator: Results › Relationship of cocaine plasma concentrations and cardiovascular effects, 2nd paragraph (pp. 1351–1352); Figs 6–7 (p. 1354); Discussion, 10th paragraph (p. 1355)

key_findings.finding: Venous concentrations after smoking were lower than in earlier studies with the same doses and pipe (about 150 and 200 ng/ml 4 minutes after a first dose of 25 or 50 mg in Foltin and Fischman, 1991); the authors attribute this to the timed 15-second smoking procedure used to match the injection, in place of the participants' usual way of smoking, and note that delivery by smoking is less consistent than by injection.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 5th paragraph (begins p. 1353, continuing on p. 1354)

key_findings.finding: The authors conclude that the arterial data do not support faster arrival at the brain as the reason for any greater effect of smoked cocaine, because arterial concentrations peaked at the same sampled time after both routes given over 15 seconds, while allowing that a larger bolus may reach the brain in the first circuit of blood after smoking.

reporting_issues.issue: F(1,7) = 5.755 is reported as P > .05 for the arterial-venous difference after injection at 20 minutes, but this F corresponds to P = .048 (editors' calculation), below the paper's own threshold of P ≤ .05; every other F statistic in the paper matches its printed P.
reporting_issues.consequence: Either the F or the P is misprinted. If the F is right, arterial and venous concentrations still differed 20 minutes after injection, and the equilibrium within 20 minutes stated in the Results and Discussion holds only for the smoked route.

reporting_issues.issue: The footnote to Table 1 gives df = 15 for regressions that, according to the Methods, use 8 participants with two doses each, and the printed P values match 15 residual df; the two entries with r² = 0.24 are smoked arterial concentration and systolic pressure at 4 minutes (P = 0.046) and injected venous concentration and high at 4 minutes (P = 0.048). By the editors' calculation, 16 observations leave 14 residual df, at which those two entries would have P of about 0.054. The two observations from each person are also treated as independent.
reporting_issues.consequence: Borderline entries in Table 1 should not be cited as significant, and all r² values describe pooled variation across doses and people rather than a within-person relationship between concentration and effect.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 1, smoked arterial concentration and diastolic pressure at 4 minutes have r² = 0.36 with P = 0.001; by the editors' calculation, with 14 to 16 df this r² gives P of about 0.009 to 0.014.
reporting_issues.consequence: Probably a misprint for about 0.01; the entry remains significant at .05.

reporting_issues.issue: The Data Analysis says the participant who did not inhale was deleted from all analyses and that peak analyses used n = 8 (p. 1348), but Figs 1–5 show N = 9 for the injected route; conversely, the drug-liking panels of Fig. 5 show N = 7 for each route, while the drug-liking F tests have 7 denominator df, implying 8 participants (p. 1350).
reporting_issues.consequence: The number of participants behind each figure and test is uncertain; the injected-route figure means include one more person than the tests.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion states that maximal arterial concentrations were at least 10-fold higher than maximal venous concentrations after either route (p. 1352), but by the editors' calculation the printed means for 32 mg injected (2347 and 252 ng/ml) give a ratio of 9.3.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the ratio of mean peaks is about 9 to 16 across doses (the other doses read approximately from Fig. 1), so about tenfold is the safer summary.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results give two magnitudes for the difference between invasive (phase II) and cuff (phase I) systolic pressure in the same paragraph: elevated by 10–15 mm Hg (p. 1348) and mean peaks 20 to 40 mm Hg higher (p. 1349); phase II pressures are given only in Fig. 3, without error bars.
reporting_issues.consequence: Phase II systolic values cannot be cited as numbers from the text; the cuff peaks of 158 and 154 mm Hg are the only printed values.

reporting_issues.issue: Placebo and sham sessions were run in every sequence but their results are neither reported in the text nor analysed, although Figs 3 and 5 show sizeable responses to sham smoking. In the editors' approximate readings of the figures, sham smoking in phase II raised mean systolic pressure from about 137 to about 165 mm Hg at the end of administration, close to the rise after 50 mg smoked (about 146 to 181 mm Hg), and produced mean high ratings of about 16.
reporting_issues.consequence: Part of the cardiovascular and rated response after smoking may come from the smoking procedure itself, so in this design the conclusion that smoked cocaine produced similar effects at lower concentrations, and the inference of a greater effect per unit concentration, cannot be separated from effects of the procedure.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion describes the ratings as showing clear dose-related effects, much clearer than the cardiovascular effects (p. 1355), whereas the Results report that medium and high doses did not differ significantly for high after either route or for stimulated after smoking (p. 1350).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the dose effect on ratings was significant only for liking (both routes) and for stimulated after injection.
